name: LEBANON
lead: Lebanon is a tiny Mediterranean country holding 6,000 years of history. Phoenicians launched ships from here carrying the world's first alphabet. Today Beirut blends Roman ruins and street-food lanes in one short walk. Snow peaks rise an hour from sunny beaches — ski and swim on the same winter day.
geo: Lebanon runs in four north–south stripes: a sunny Mediterranean coast, the towering Mount Lebanon range, the flat Bekaa Valley, and the Anti-Lebanon mountains on the Syrian border. The Bekaa catches water from both ranges, making it Lebanon's bread-basket.

The Kadisha Valley, carved into the northern mountains, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site where monks sheltered in cliff-face caves for centuries. Cedar groves protected above 1,400 m shelter trees over a thousand years old.
animals: The Lebanon cedar (Cedrus libani) is the living national emblem — ancient trees in the Shouf reserve spread wide flat canopies like giant green parasols. Striped hyenas, wild boar, and stone martens roam the mountain forests after dark.

Loggerhead sea turtles nest on Lebanon's sandy beaches each summer. Every autumn, soaring flocks of migrating raptors — honey buzzards and short-toed eagles — funnel through the mountain ridges in spectacular rivers of wings.
culture: Lebanese food is famous worldwide: meze spreads of hummus, tabbouleh, and warm flatbread cover every table before the main dish arrives. Hospitality is a point of national pride — guests receive cardamom coffee the moment they walk through the door.

The dabke is a stomping line-dance performed at weddings, dancers linking arms and kicking in perfect unison. The Baalbeck International Festival — inside colossal Roman ruins — has hosted opera and jazz since 1956.
history: Phoenicians founded trading cities here around 3000 BCE, spreading the world's first widely-used alphabet to Greece and beyond. Alexander the Great, Romans, Crusaders, and Ottomans each left temples, castles, or boulevards still walkable today.

Lebanon gained independence from France in 1943. A civil war (1975–1990) split Beirut along the Green Line, but the city rebuilt dramatically. Baalbek's Roman temples have stood through 2,000 years of earthquakes and invasions.
wows: Phoenicians invented the 22-letter alphabet that became the root of Greek, Latin, and Arabic writing.
You can ski Mzaar in the morning and swim in the Mediterranean that same afternoon — just 50 km apart.
Baalbek's Trilithon foundation holds three stones each weighing up to 1,000 tonnes — moved without machines.
Byblos has been continuously inhabited since ~5000 BCE — one of the oldest cities on Earth.
The Lebanese diaspora of ~14 million worldwide is more than double the home population.
Tyre was built on an island; Alexander filled the sea with a km-long causeway in 332 BCE — still there.
Egyptian pharaohs sent entire fleets to Lebanon to buy cedar wood for royal ships and temples.

myths.fact: Lebanon gets heavy mountain snow from December to April. Ski resorts, lush valleys, and reliable rainfall make it one of the greenest countries in the Middle East.
Lebanese Arabic naturally blends Arabic, French, and English mid-sentence. This code-switching sounds unlike any other Arabic dialect spoken elsewhere.
